title: T4.4: Implements Concurrency Controls
description: Test your knowledge of concurrency control mechanisms in InterSystems IRIS, including locking, best practices, and choosing between row-level and table-level locks

questions.question: What is the purpose of the LOCK command in InterSystems IRIS?

options.text: To prevent all database access during critical operations
To create an exclusive reference to a specific global node for synchronization
To automatically commit pending transactions
To disable concurrent SQL queries on a table

questions.explanation: The LOCK command creates an exclusive reference to a specific global node, allowing processes to synchronize access to shared resources. When a process executes LOCK ^GlobalName(subscript), it attempts to acquire an exclusive lock on that reference. Other processes attempting to lock the same reference will wait until the lock is released. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: After executing a LOCK command, which special variable should you check to determine if the lock was successfully acquired?

options.text: $HOROLOG
$TEST
$LOCK
$STATUS

questions.explanation: The $TEST special variable is set to 1 (true) if the LOCK command successfully acquired the lock, or 0 (false) if it failed (when using a timeout). After executing LOCK with a timeout, you should check IF $TEST to determine whether the lock was acquired before proceeding with critical operations. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: What happens when you execute a LOCK command without any arguments?

options.text: It throws an error
It releases all locks held by the current process
It acquires a global database lock
It displays currently held locks

questions.explanation: Executing LOCK with no arguments releases all locks currently held by the process. This is a common pattern at the end of a critical section or before process termination to ensure locks are not inadvertently held. LOCK without arguments is equivalent to 'unlock all'. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: Which LOCK syntax adds a new lock while preserving existing locks held by the process?

options.text: LOCK ^NewLock
LOCK +^NewLock
LOCK &^NewLock
LOCK *^NewLock

questions.explanation: The LOCK + (incremental lock) syntax adds a new lock while preserving existing locks. LOCK +^NewLock acquires a lock on ^NewLock without releasing previously held locks. In contrast, LOCK ^NewLock releases all existing locks before acquiring the new one. The + operator is essential for acquiring multiple locks simultaneously. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: Which of the following are best practices for using LOCK commands in InterSystems IRIS?

options.text: Always specify a timeout value to prevent indefinite waits
Use the same lock reference names consistently across all processes
Hold locks for the minimum time necessary to complete the critical operation
Lock entire globals rather than specific subscripted nodes for better performance
Check $TEST after LOCK with timeout to verify acquisition

questions.explanation: Best practices include: (1) Always use timeout values to prevent processes from waiting indefinitely; (2) Use consistent lock naming conventions across the application; (3) Hold locks for the shortest time possible to minimize contention; (4) Check $TEST after timeout-based locks. Locking entire globals is NOT recommended as it creates unnecessary contention - lock only the specific nodes needed. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question:
Scenario: Two users access the same record in a stateless web application. Both users edit the data independently and attempt to save their changes. The application must ensure that changes made by one user are not overwritten by the other without detection.

Question: Which approach is most appropriate for managing concurrency in this scenario?

options.text: Use optimistic concurrency with a version counter to detect and reject conflicting updates
Use pessimistic concurrency to lock the record for the first user, preventing the second user from editing
Allow both users to make updates, and the last save overwrites any earlier changes
Use a SQL table to implement pessimistic concurrency with long-duration locks

questions.explanation: Optimistic concurrency with a version counter is the most appropriate approach for stateless web applications. Each record includes a version field that is incremented with each update. When saving, the application checks if the version matches the original; if not, another user has modified the record. This approach works well in stateless environments where holding locks across HTTP requests is impractical. Pessimistic locking is unsuitable for stateless applications as locks cannot be maintained between requests. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ_concurrency

questions.question: What is the primary difference between row-level locks and table-level locks in SQL?

options.text: Row-level locks are faster but use more memory
Row-level locks allow concurrent access to different rows, while table-level locks prevent all concurrent access to the table
Table-level locks are only available in embedded SQL
Row-level locks require manual LOCK commands, while table-level locks are automatic

questions.explanation: Row-level locks allow multiple processes to access different rows in the same table concurrently, maximizing concurrency. Table-level locks prevent all concurrent access to the entire table during the lock duration, which can significantly reduce concurrency but may be appropriate for operations affecting many rows. The choice depends on the operation scope and concurrency requirements. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RSQL_locktable

questions.question: Which SQL isolation level provides the highest degree of concurrency by allowing dirty reads?

options.text: READ UNCOMMITTED
READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ
SERIALIZABLE

questions.explanation: READ UNCOMMITTED provides the highest concurrency by allowing dirty reads (reading uncommitted changes from other transactions). This isolation level sacrifices data consistency for performance and concurrency. It's appropriate for reporting or analytics where approximate data is acceptable. Higher isolation levels (READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE) provide stronger consistency guarantees but reduce concurrency. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RSQL_set#RSQL_set_transaction

questions.question: In ObjectScript, what is the correct syntax to acquire an incremental lock with a 5-second timeout, preserving existing locks?

options.text: LOCK ^MyLock TIMEOUT 5
LOCK +^MyLock:5
LOCK ^MyLock(5)
LOCK ^MyLock WAIT 5

questions.explanation: The correct syntax for an incremental lock with timeout is LOCK +lockref:timeout. LOCK +^MyLock:5 attempts to acquire the lock while preserving any existing locks, waiting up to 5 seconds. The + is important: without it (LOCK ^MyLock:5), all existing locks would be released first. If the lock cannot be acquired within 5 seconds, $TEST is set to 0 and execution continues. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: When should you consider using table-level locks instead of row-level locks?

options.text: When performing bulk operations affecting most or all rows in a table
When you need to prevent all concurrent modifications during a complex transaction
When performing a single-row SELECT query
When you need to maintain referential integrity across multiple tables
When rebuilding indexes or performing table maintenance

questions.explanation: Table-level locks are appropriate for: (1) Bulk operations affecting many/all rows where row-level locks would be inefficient; (2) Complex transactions requiring table-wide consistency; (3) Maintenance operations like index rebuilds. Single-row queries should use row-level locks for better concurrency. Referential integrity is typically managed through constraints, not table locks. Table-level locks reduce concurrency significantly, so use them only when necessary. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RSQL_locktable

questions.question: What happens if a process terminates abnormally while holding locks?

options.text: The locks remain indefinitely, requiring manual intervention
Other processes waiting for those locks will receive an error
InterSystems IRIS automatically releases all locks held by the terminated process
The database becomes corrupted and must be restored

questions.explanation: InterSystems IRIS automatically releases all locks held by a process when that process terminates, whether normally or abnormally. This prevents deadlock situations where locks would be held indefinitely. Processes waiting for those locks will then be able to acquire them. This automatic cleanup is a critical safety feature of the locking mechanism. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: Which SQL command explicitly acquires a table-level lock?

options.text: LOCK TABLE table_name
SET LOCK TABLE table_name
ACQUIRE LOCK ON table_name
BEGIN TRANSACTION WITH LOCK

questions.explanation: The LOCK TABLE statement explicitly acquires a table-level lock in SQL. Syntax: LOCK TABLE table_name IN {SHARE|EXCLUSIVE} MODE. SHARE mode allows concurrent reads but prevents writes. EXCLUSIVE mode prevents all concurrent access. Table locks are held until the transaction ends (COMMIT or ROLLBACK). Use table locks sparingly as they significantly reduce concurrency. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RSQL_locktable

questions.question: What is the effect of executing LOCK -^MyLock in ObjectScript?

options.text: It acquires an exclusive lock on ^MyLock
It releases the lock on ^MyLock while maintaining other locks
It acquires a shared (read-only) lock on ^MyLock
It throws a syntax error

questions.explanation: The LOCK - (decremental unlock) syntax releases a specific lock while preserving other locks held by the process. LOCK -^MyLock releases only the lock on ^MyLock; any other locks remain active. This is useful when you need to release locks selectively. In contrast, LOCK without arguments releases all locks. The + and - operators allow fine-grained lock management. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: Which statements about optimistic concurrency control are TRUE?

options.text: It assumes conflicts are rare and detects them at save time
It requires holding locks throughout the edit session
It typically uses version numbers or timestamps to detect conflicts
It is well-suited for stateless web applications
It prevents conflicts by blocking concurrent access

questions.explanation: Optimistic concurrency: (1) Assumes conflicts are rare and checks for them only when saving; (2) Does NOT hold locks during editing - data is read without locks; (3) Uses version counters, timestamps, or checksums to detect if data changed since it was read; (4) Works well in stateless environments like web apps where maintaining locks across requests is impractical. Pessimistic concurrency, not optimistic, prevents conflicts by blocking concurrent access with locks. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ_concurrency

questions.question: In a high-concurrency OLTP system, you need to update individual customer records. Which approach provides the best balance of data integrity and concurrency?

options.text: Use table-level exclusive locks for all customer updates
Use row-level locks with appropriate isolation levels
Disable all locking for maximum performance
Use optimistic concurrency without any locks

questions.explanation: Row-level locks with appropriate isolation levels provide the best balance for high-concurrency OLTP systems updating individual records. They ensure data integrity while allowing maximum concurrency - multiple processes can update different customer records simultaneously. Table-level locks would serialize all updates, severely limiting throughput. Disabling locks risks data corruption. Optimistic concurrency works for stateless apps but may not be suitable for all OLTP scenarios, especially where conflicts are common. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RSQL_locktable

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to acquire a shared lock on a global node in ObjectScript?

options.text: LOCK +^Data(id) SHARED
LOCK +^Data(id)#"S"
LOCK +^Data(id):"shared"
LOCK SHARED +^Data(id)

questions.explanation: To acquire a shared lock, use the #"S" lock type modifier. The syntax LOCK +^Data(id)#"S" acquires a shared lock on the specified node. Multiple processes can hold the same shared lock simultaneously, but a shared lock prevents exclusive locks and vice versa. Shared locks are useful when multiple processes need to read data while preventing other processes from modifying it. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: Within a transaction, you execute LOCK -^Data(1) to release a lock. When is the lock actually released by default?

options.text: Immediately when LOCK -^Data(1) executes
At the end of the transaction (TCOMMIT or TROLLBACK)
When the process terminates
After a 30-second delay

questions.explanation: By default, when you unlock a non-incremented lock within a transaction, InterSystems IRIS maintains that lock in a 'delock state' until the end of the transaction. This ensures transactional integrity - if the transaction rolls back, the lock protection was maintained throughout. To immediately release a lock within a transaction, use the #"I" (immediate) modifier: LOCK -^Data(1)#"I". Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: Within a transaction, what does the #"I" lock type modifier do when releasing a lock?

options.text: It acquires an incremental lock
It immediately releases the lock, bypassing the default deferred-until-TCOMMIT behavior
It converts the lock to an implicit lock
It makes the lock invisible to other processes

questions.explanation: The #"I" (immediate) modifier forces immediate release of a lock within a transaction. By default, when you unlock within a transaction, the lock enters a 'delock state' and is not actually released until TCOMMIT or TROLLBACK. Using LOCK -^Data(id)#"I" immediately releases the lock regardless of transaction state. Use this when you need to release a lock before transaction completion, but be aware this may affect transactional integrity. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: Which statements about shared locks (#"S") in InterSystems IRIS are TRUE?

options.text: Multiple processes can hold the same shared lock simultaneously
A shared lock prevents exclusive locks on the same resource
An exclusive lock prevents shared locks on the same resource
Shared locks are automatically upgraded to exclusive locks when needed
Shared locks are useful for read-only access while preventing writes

questions.explanation: Shared locks allow multiple readers while preventing writers: (1) Multiple processes can hold the same shared lock; (2) A shared lock blocks exclusive locks; (3) An exclusive lock blocks shared locks; (4) They're ideal for viewing data while preventing edits. Shared locks are NOT automatically upgraded - you must explicitly release the shared lock and acquire an exclusive one. This is a common pattern: acquire shared lock to read, release it, acquire exclusive lock to write. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question:
Consider this code:

```
TSTART
LOCK +^Customer(id):5
IF '$TEST { TROLLBACK  QUIT 0 }
SET ^Customer(id,"Balance")=newBalance
LOCK -^Customer(id)
DO AuditLog(id, newBalance)
TCOMMIT
QUIT 1
```

What is the problem with this lock management?

options.text: The lock timeout is too short
The lock is released before TCOMMIT but remains in delock state, which is correct
The lock should use #"S" for shared access
LOCK -^Customer(id) should come after TCOMMIT

questions.explanation: The code is actually correct! When LOCK -^Customer(id) executes within the transaction, the lock enters a 'delock state' and is not actually released until TCOMMIT. This is the default behavior that ensures transactional integrity - the lock protection is maintained throughout the transaction. If the AuditLog call fails and causes TROLLBACK, the lock was still held during the entire critical section. This is intentional design, not a problem. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: Two processes are experiencing deadlock. Process A holds lock ^Data(1) and waits for ^Data(2). Process B holds lock ^Data(2) and waits for ^Data(1). What is the best practice to prevent this?

options.text: Use shorter timeout values on all locks
Always acquire multiple locks in a consistent, predetermined order
Use shared locks instead of exclusive locks
Disable locking for one of the processes

questions.explanation: The best practice for deadlock prevention is to acquire locks in a consistent order across all processes. If both processes always lock ^Data(1) before ^Data(2), deadlock cannot occur. This is a fundamental principle of concurrent programming. Shorter timeouts don't prevent deadlock (they just make detection faster). Shared locks don't help if both need exclusive access. Disabling locking risks data corruption. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question: What is the purpose of the ^$LOCK structured system variable?

options.text: To acquire locks on multiple globals simultaneously
To query information about locks currently held by processes
To configure global lock timeout settings
To release all locks in the system

questions.explanation: The ^$LOCK structured system variable allows you to query information about locks currently held by processes in the system. You can iterate through ^$LOCK to see which locks exist, which process holds each lock, the lock type (shared/exclusive), and the lock count. This is invaluable for debugging concurrency issues and monitoring lock contention. Syntax examples: $DATA(^$LOCK(lockref)) checks if a lock exists; $ORDER(^$LOCK(prev)) iterates through locks. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_slock

questions.question: What does the CONCURRENCY class parameter control in a persistent class?

options.text: The maximum number of concurrent users who can access the class
The default locking behavior when objects of the class are accessed
Whether the class supports multi-threading
The transaction isolation level for SQL queries

questions.explanation: The CONCURRENCY class parameter (also known as DEFAULTCONCURRENCY) specifies the default locking behavior for persistent objects. Values include: 0 (no locking), 1 (atomic - lock during save only), 2 (shared lock while object is open), 3 (shared lock retained after close), 4 (exclusive lock while open). This setting applies when methods like %Open() or %Save() don't specify a concurrency argument. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ_concurrency

questions.question: What is the purpose of the #"E" (escalating) lock type?

options.text: To automatically elevate user privileges when acquiring locks
To allow the lock to be automatically promoted from row-level to table-level based on lock count
To enable emergency lock acquisition bypassing normal wait times
To create an encrypted lock reference

questions.explanation: The #"E" escalating lock type enables automatic lock escalation. When many individual row-level locks are acquired (exceeding a threshold), they can be automatically promoted to a single table-level lock. This reduces lock table overhead when a transaction affects many rows. Use LOCK +^Table(row)#"E" for escalating locks. The escalation threshold is configurable. This is useful for operations that may touch many rows but shouldn't hold thousands of individual locks. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=RCOS_clock

questions.question:
Consider this pattern for implementing read-then-update with proper locking:

```
; Step 1: Read with shared lock
LOCK +^Data(id)#"S":5
IF '$TEST QUIT "Lock failed"
SET value = ^Data(id)
LOCK -^Data(id)#"S"

; Step 2: Modify value...
SET newValue = value + 100

; Step 3: Write with exclusive lock
LOCK +^Data(id):5
IF '$TEST QUIT "Lock failed"
; Verify value unchanged
IF ^Data(id)'=value {
    LOCK -^Data(id)
    QUIT "Concurrency conflict"
}
SET ^Data(id) = newValue
LOCK -^Data(id)
QUIT "Success"
```

What concurrency pattern does this implement?

options.text: Pessimistic locking with shared-to-exclusive upgrade
Optimistic concurrency control with version verification
Two-phase locking protocol
Lock-free concurrent programming

questions.explanation: This implements optimistic concurrency control. The pattern: (1) Read with shared lock to get current value, (2) Release lock and do processing, (3) Acquire exclusive lock and verify value hasn't changed before updating. If the value changed (another process modified it), the update is rejected. This allows high concurrency during the read/process phase while still detecting conflicts at write time. The verification step (IF ^Data(id)'=value) is the optimistic check. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GOBJ_concurrency

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the InterSystems IRIS Work Queue Manager?

options.text: To acquire exclusive locks on database globals for concurrent safety
To distribute independent work units across multiple background worker jobs for parallel execution
To serialize all write operations through a single background job
To replace the use of LOCK commands in multi-process applications

questions.explanation: The Work Queue Manager (%SYSTEM.WorkMgr) is designed to parallelize work by distributing independent units across a pool of worker jobs. It is not a locking or serialization mechanism — those are provided by the LOCK command and transactions. WQM is intended for CPU-bound or I/O-bound batch work that can be decomposed into independent units. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GWORK_intro

questions.question: What is the correct basic workflow for using the Work Queue Manager?

options.text: Call Queue() multiple times, then call Initialize() once at the end
Call Initialize() to get a queue handle, call Queue() for each work unit, then call Sync() to wait for completion
Call Sync() first to reserve workers, then call Queue() for each work item
Call $SYSTEM.WorkMgr.Run() with an array of work items as the single argument

questions.explanation: The standard workflow is: (1) obtain a queue handle with Set queue = $SYSTEM.WorkMgr.Initialize(,.sc); (2) submit work items repeatedly with queue.Queue("ClassName.Method", args...); (3) wait for all work to complete with queue.Sync() or queue.WaitForComplete(timeout). Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GWORK_intro

questions.question: What is the difference between Sync() and WaitForComplete() on a Work Queue Manager queue?

options.text: Sync() waits for all queued work to complete; WaitForComplete() does the same but accepts a timeout parameter
Sync() runs work serially; WaitForComplete() runs work in parallel
Sync() commits a transaction; WaitForComplete() does not touch transactions
They are identical — WaitForComplete() is an alias for Sync()

questions.explanation: Both methods block until all queued work items complete and return the overall status. The key difference is that WaitForComplete(timeout) accepts a timeout parameter, whereas Sync() waits indefinitely. Use WaitForComplete when you need to bound the total wait time. A related method, WaitOne(timeout), returns as soon as any single item finishes. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GWORK_intro

questions.question: When do Setup and Teardown callbacks run on a Work Queue Manager queue?

options.text: Before and after each individual work item, inside the same worker job
Once per worker job — Setup runs before the first item, Teardown after the last item that worker processes
Only on the calling process, never on the worker jobs
Setup runs on the master, Teardown runs when Sync() returns

questions.explanation: Setup and Teardown callbacks are per-worker, not per-work-item. A worker runs Setup once before processing its first item, then processes all items assigned to it, then runs Teardown once after the last item. This lets you amortize expensive per-worker initialization such as opening database connections or loading configuration. Running them per item would defeat the performance purpose. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GWORK_setup_teardown

questions.question: Which of the following are best practices when using the Work Queue Manager? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Make each work unit fully self-contained with no shared mutable state between units
Pass all needed data as arguments to Queue() rather than relying on variables from the calling process
Always check the status returned by Sync() to detect errors in work items
Use Work Queue Manager for every request, including interactive sub-second operations, to maximize parallelism
Keep work unit size large enough to amortize the per-job startup overhead

questions.explanation: Valid best practices: work units must be independent (no shared mutable state); data must be passed as Queue() arguments since worker jobs don't inherit caller variables; always check the Sync() return status for work-item errors; unit work should be large enough that the cost of starting a worker job is amortized. WQM is NOT appropriate for sub-second interactive requests — the job-creation overhead outweighs any parallelism gain. Reference: https://docs.intersystems.com/irislatest/csp/docbook/DocBook.UI.Page.cls?KEY=GWORK_intro
